organizations.name: al-Qaeda
organizations.notes: Has not publicly named a successor to Zawahiri. Hosts give four non-exclusive reasons: security protocol, avoiding embarrassing the Taliban, the leader's possible Iran base, or that a leader is already chosen but unannounced. No branch has disavowed it.

organizations.name: Taliban
organizations.notes: Denied then 'investigated' Zawahiri's presence in Kabul. Hosts say it benefits from de facto legitimacy and has an arrangement with al-Qaeda.

organizations.name: Haqqani Network
organizations.notes: Described as the al-Qaeda-linked, allied subgroup/faction of the Taliban led by Sirajuddin Haqqani.

organizations.name: al-Shabaab
organizations.notes: Described as 'the Taliban of Africa' and al-Qaeda's best organized branch. It has suppressed the Islamic State in Somalia and manipulates clan politics. It struck at the Hayat Hotel and Beledweyne.

organizations.name: Islamic State
organizations.notes: Could exploit an al-Qaeda emir being based in Iran; the hosts say it does so mainly in al-Naba.

organizations.name: Hayat Tahrir al-Sham
organizations.notes: Former al-Qaeda members now in HTS urge AQ members to leave AQ; the hosts see this as poaching and a bid for legitimacy for HTS's statelet in northwest Syria.

organizations.name: AQAP
organizations.notes: Cited as a branch that publicly announces new emirs.

organizations.name: AQIM
organizations.notes: Cited as a branch that publicly announces new emirs.

organizations.name: Tehrik-e-Taliban Pakistan
aliases: the movement of the Taliban in Pakistan
organizations.notes: Said to have emerged from al-Qaeda's work navigating tribal dynamics in Pakistan's tribal areas.

organizations.name: Somali National Army
organizations.notes: Leads clearing operations in the offensive that began in mid-September 2022.

organizations.name: Ma'awisley
organizations.notes: Clan-based militias of citizens fed up with Shabaab, now armed and mobilized by the state. Compared to the Awakening/Sons of Iraq. They do holding operations.

organizations.name: ATMIS
aliases: African Union Transition Mission in Somalia
organizations.notes: Successor to AMISOM; gives medical and medevac support and sets up joint operation centers with the SNA.

organizations.name: AMISOM
organizations.notes: Predecessor of ATMIS.

organizations.name: Djiboutian troops
organizations.notes: Allegedly give mechanized support to the SNA in Hiraan, which is the Djibouti-held sector.

organizations.name: United States
organizations.notes: Killed Zawahiri in Kabul. Conducted two airstrikes in Somalia during the offensive (a 'defensive' strike killing 27 and the strike that killed Abdullah Yare). Special Forces are back in Somalia in an advisory capacity.

organizations.name: Jubaland
organizations.notes: Expected to launch an offensive against Shabaab. Weiss speculates that this could push Shabaab fighters into Kenya.

organizations.name: Federal Government of Somalia
organizations.notes: Issued a statement that sharing Shabaab propaganda violates Somalia's terrorism act. Accounts were banned, and the hosts worry that journalists and analysts may be caught up in the ban.

organizations.name: Kenya Defence Forces
organizations.notes: Its base at El Adde was routed by Shabaab in 2016; Kenya downplayed it.

organizations.name: Rewards for Justice
organizations.notes: Offered a $3 million bounty on Abdullah Yare.

organizations.name: Burundian troops
organizations.notes: Their base in Middle Shabelle was overrun by Shabaab earlier in 2022. Burundi downplayed it and has still not given a full casualty estimate.

organizations.name: Puntland
organizations.notes: Northern semi-autonomous region that de facto controls an area disputed with Somaliland. Shabaab carried out a suicide bombing there.

organizations.name: Somaliland
organizations.notes: The territory it claims saw the first Shabaab suicide bombing since 2018.

organizations.name: Long War Journal
organizations.notes: Banned in Pakistan for about 10 years, and the hosts worry it could also be banned in Somalia.

organizations.name: Al-Qaeda in Iraq
organizations.notes: Roggio cites its propaganda as essential for understanding Anbar province.

events.description: US airstrike (most likely a drone) kills Ayman al-Zawahiri in Kabul at the end of July 2022; he was sheltered by Sirajuddin Haqqani's network.
US raid kills Osama bin Laden; al-Qaeda took about six weeks to announce a successor.
Shabaab figure pledges allegiance to bin Laden on behalf of the group; al-Qaeda never officially responded and told Shabaab to keep it quiet.
Zawahiri, as al-Qaeda emir, decides to make the Shabaab oath of allegiance public, against bin Laden's earlier policy. The year is inferred, not stated.
During the 2010-2011 drought, Shabaab downplayed its al-Qaeda ties while distributing foreign aid, yet featured American al-Qaeda member Jehad Mostafa at aid events.
Shabaab lays siege to the Hayat Hotel in Mogadishu for more than 30 hours, killing dozens, its longest hotel siege in the city.
After the hotel siege, Hassan Sheikh Mohamud vows to defeat Shabaab within one year.
Somalia launches the largest offensive against Shabaab since about 2011 in mid-September, led by the SNA and Ma'awisley with ATMIS and US support, in Hiraan, Galgaduud and Bay.
US 'defensive' airstrike in support of Somali forces in contact allegedly kills 27 Shabaab fighters.
US airstrike kills Shabaab co-founder and Dawa head Abdullah Yare, who had a $3 million bounty.
Shabaab spokesman Ali Rage releases a video accepting Hassan Sheikh's challenge to face the government head on.
Triple suicide bombing in Beledweyne hits a clan-fighter mobilization center, then emergency responders; about 30 or more killed.
Somalia reports new offensive operations in Middle Shabelle; Shabaab retaliates, claiming to have killed Ugandan and Burundian troops.
Ahmed Madobe announces Jubaland forces will soon start their own counteroffensive against Shabaab.
The Somali government bans accounts it deems Shabaab propaganda, citing its terrorism act, which risks catching analysts and journalists.
Shabaab routs a Kenyan KDF base at El Adde; Kenya downplayed it until Shabaab released video and photos.
The Somali federal government stated that sharing Shabaab propaganda violates its terrorism act and banned many accounts.
Shabaab routed a Kenyan base at el-Adde. Kenya initially denied the attack, then downplayed it.
Shabaab overran a Burundian base in Middle Shabelle and killed dozens of troops.
Shabaab incursion into Ethiopia early in the year.
Shabaab suicide bombing in Somaliland-claimed territory controlled de facto by Puntland, the first in that territory since 2018.

key_claims: The current offensive is the biggest threat Shabaab has faced since 2011, according to Weiss.
Shabaab habitually makes tactical retreats, withdrawing from one area and appearing in another.
A Jubaland offensive could push Shabaab fighters into northeast Kenya or Ethiopia.
Shabaab has expanded into northern Somalia, as shown by the first suicide bombing in Somaliland-claimed territory since 2018.
Kenya and Burundi both initially denied or downplayed Shabaab victories, and Shabaab's photos and videos later contradicted them.
Somalia's broad ban on sharing Shabaab propaganda could catch journalists and analysts, though the hosts support the government.
